articleTitle: Harmonics-causes, effects, measurements and analysis-update
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Modern technology has made possible the rectification of AC power to DC power using static rectifiers for DC drives as well as static inversion for AC drives. Rectification generates harmonic voltages and currents which can cause problems, e.g.: insulation failures due to overheating and overvoltages; malfunction of solid-state equipment; and communication interference. In the present work, the authors describe a field-proven, portable, harmonic measurement/analysis system for monitoring such harmonic voltages and currents. This computer-based system provides on-site data collection, precise harmonic identification via a fast Fourier transform, data analysis, and report preparation via a custom spreadsheet. Specific examples involving the application of this measurement/analysis system in the cement, steel, and carbon industries are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experience of the high pressure roller press installation at Coplay Cement's Nazareth I Plant
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The object of the roller press installation was to add sufficient grinding capacity to the Nazareth I finish mill system to warrant the building of an on-site packing facility, which would then allow the closure of the satellite plant and eliminate the need for costly shipments of clinker and maintenance of the two older finish mill systems that are presently operating at the satellite facility. The major modifications, experiences, and results of the installation are presented. The roller press has achieved up to 70 stph increase on type I cement. This corresponds to an investment cost of only $42000 per short ton of capacity. To this can be added the energy savings of 30% or 15 kWh per short tone. This reduction in energy consumption also reduces the total specific plant power costs and together with off-peak grinding results in savings of over $500000 per year.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The need for power system studies increase with the use of adjustable speed drive
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author reviews the various system studies that are performed on industrial power systems and discusses the advantages and information obtained from these studies. Case studies of applications are used to illustrate some findings from the studies of systems with adjustable-speed drives. It is noted that system studies for short-circuit protective device coordination, load flow, and motor starting have long proved valuable. More recently, the influence of nonlinear loads, in particular adjustable-speed drives, on the power system with the application of power factor improvement capacitors has given rise to problems with harmonic currents and voltages. This study provides two solutions to power system problems: the improvement of the power factor of the plant load and the control of the resonant point in the system which in turn controls the flow of the harmonic current produced by static power converters as used in adjustable-speed drives.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Trends in LANs for plant automation
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The use of local area networks (LANs) for plant automation is discussed. Consideration is given to the use of communication networks as integration tools, LAN services, network types, the solution of the integration problem, the Open System Interconnection model, the IEEE 802 project, upper-layer standards, the MAP (manufacturing automation protocol) support of more than one network type. process control influence on MAP, and standard and proprietary LANs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer integrated manufacturing: a case study in the cement industry
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: CalMat has recently made a concerted effort at decreasing manufacturing costs and increasing productivity throughout the cement division. One aspect of these efforts has involved the planning for and the application of computer integrated manufacturing (CIM) to provide managers at all levels with the tools and information they need to achieve these dual goals. The CIM effort has been directed at both corporate and plant functions and includes both manufacturing and support personnel. The breadth of the hardware installation has ranged from complete new distributed control systems to corporatewide data communications networks and individual personal computers and workstations. Applications software has ranged from typical motor control logic and direct digital control algorithms to distributed databases and expert systems. The author uses a generic CIM model to summarize work to date in three cement plants constructed or modernized over the last 25 years and to highlight directions for the future. Special emphasis is placed on the identifying the areas of highest return for CIM in the cement industry, and the practical and political pitfalls of implementing CIM in any manufacturing environment are discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Supervisory control applied to a cement kiln incinerating recovered solvent
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The National Cement Company of California has kept pace with developments in the industry with a combination of fuel selection and other capital improvements. In 1982, the plant began burning industrial-waste solvents in addition to petroleum coke. In 1988, a LINKman supervisory control system was added which, in addition to the normal high-level control functions, provided additional facilities to manage their multiple fuels. A major consideration is the balancing of different fuels of varying heat content while maintaining an ideal mix from economic, legal, and chemical standpoints. The LINKman high-level control system has proven effective in enabling the plant operations personnel to deal effectively with these challenges. It has been instrumental in their efforts to obtain a modified permit, allowing them to double their use of recovered solvent fuel. The control strategy is continually reviewed and modified in order to adapt to changing plant conditions and economic considerations.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PC-based diagnostic tool for predictive maintenance of cement mill equipment
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: A PC-based monitoring system has been developed to monitor motor drives used by the cement industry. The system uses a versatile front-end data-acquisition system that can interface with a variety of transducers. The system can be used to provide information about the condition of motors and other equipment. Monitoring system hardware, software, and applications are described. This integrated tool is capable of being expanded for plantwide monitoring. The principal advantage is that monitoring can be done in a cost-effective manner. All critical parameters are continuously monitored, so that any problems can be detected and corrected at early stages, leading to better equipment utilization and life. Information gathered by the signal conditioning and event monitoring system provides a database of trends that is very valuable for design engineers in developing better and more cost-effective machines and systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrated electrical power monitoring systems
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The authors describe a system (called Epic Microversatrip) that integrates metering, protection (direct acting breaker trips or relaying), monitoring, and fault analysis in electrical switchgear. With this system not only can individual conventional meters, instruments, discrete transducers, and protective relays be replaced, but added functions can be provided. The total system then provides an economical alternative for determining the pulse of the electrical power distribution system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Dynamic problems of girth gear drives for ball mills in the cement industry
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is noted that two essential factors influence the operating behavior of girth gear drives, namely the dynamic behavior of the drive train and the load distribution along the tooth flanks. These operating parameters can be analyzed by means of field measurements with the application of strain gauges, and the measured figures can be used for setting up suitable calculation models. This enables operating conditions to be simulated and the individual components of the drive system to be mutually matched in an optimum way. By means of examples from practice the authors explain how the causes of damage can be determined by a combination of computer analysis and measurements for the entire system and how remedial action can be taken.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Industrial coal-fired explosion hazards
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Coal safety requirements in the cement industry are discussed. Safety requirements associated with coal grinding, drying, blending, transporting, and storing are also examined. Case histories investigated by the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) are discussed, and recommendations are made for future fire and explosion prevention.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Unloading bulk cement ships
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The vacuum unloading system for the Tampa, Florida cement plant is described, and its operation and maintenance are discussed. It is concluded that the vacuum unloading system is a sound concept and, with the proper sizing of equipment and arrangement of facilities, can accomplish all that is needed in a ship unloading system. Environmentally, it has met the rigid requirements at Tampa, which was a major consideration in the selection of a system. A schematic diagram and pictures of the Tampa unloading operation are included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Developing specifications for cement plant automation systems
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author discusses the key guidelines that produce a good specification for cement plant automation systems, reviews how to organize the specification effort, and examines what makes it work. He describes the keys to a smooth and problem-free specification development project. He then elaborates major pitfalls in developing specifications and makes suggestions about how to avoid them.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modernizing the finish grinding systems at Heidelberg's Leimen Plant
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The second high-pressure grinding roll installed at Heidelberg's Leimen Plant, based on experience with the first industrial pilot installation, has demonstrated that six different types of cement with different feed compositions and different finenesses can be produced in a single grinding system utilizing recirculation of separator rejects and flakes. Capacity increases of the existing ball milling circuit have been reached in the hybrid grinding mode as well as with flake recirculation ranging between 16 and 45%. These capacity increases are in line with figures based on previous experience in this plant. Energy savings achieved range from approximately 2 to 7.5 kWh/MT, which also is in the range of previous experience.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The personal computer and fault studies power systems
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author discusses what should be desirable features in any power system fault analysis program and the traps that can occur. Particular attention is given to software and hardware selection and to the use of the program. Possible future trends in this area are examined. A software selection guide is then presented along with an example.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experiences with adjustable AC drives in a cement plant
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author highlights the basic requirements to be considered when specifying a complete drive package with a rating up to 500 hp at 460 V AC. Applications currently in use at the Dundee Michigan cement plant along with the corresponding operating experiences are discussed. The following issues are discussed in connection with the complete drive package: location of drive; enclosure type and size; control strategy; standardization of drives; training; and harmonics.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Torsional vibration calculation and analysis of tube mills
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is noted that torsional vibration considerations of the tube mill are very important for the normal operation and design of tube-mill drive systems. The theoretical basis for obtaining mathematical models of the mill torsional-vibration system is discussed. The dynamic parameters of the practice tube-mill system in cement plants are calculated by using state-space representation and complex modal analysis techniques. Also examined is the damping of tube-mill torsional vibration, including such techniques as electromagnetic damping, oil damping, and grinding medium damping. It is shown that these dampings have a powerful effect on the dynamic response of the mill drive system. Experimental research performed on tube-mill systems in cement plants is also reported. The test data and calculated results are shown to agree very well.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modernization of the Heartland Cement Plant
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Two major renovations at the Heartland Cement Company in Independence, Kansas are described. First, the coal grinding system was converted to indirect-field, with new instrumentation to make the system more dependable and efficient. Second, the raw meal grinding and drying system, which consisted of a large array of outdated inefficient equipment, was completely replaced by a single vertical roller mill to reduce maintenance and power consumption, while improving product quality. Benefits of the coal mill modernization include better coal grinding, drying, and firing control, with a 10% decrease in fuel consumption. The new system has dramatically reduced labor, electrical, and fuel costs, while enhancing burnability and allowing the kilns to produce a higher-quality clinker.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Bulk cement-ship unloaders
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The ship unloading system for the Mississauga Cement Plant in Southern Ontario is discussed. Criteria for the choice of the unloading equipment are examined, and the selected system and its operation are described. It is concluded that the vertical-screw type of unloading equipment has performed extremely well. The cost of operating the equipment has remained well within the expected limits. Numerous photographs illustrating the operation of the unloading system are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improved fuel efficiency with a direct-fired system
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The successful experience with the installation of a TAS Systems micronizing coal mill at Ideal's Tijeras, New Mexico plant and Devil's Slide, Utah plant is described. The TAS system was developed on the understanding that micronized coal is more reactive than pulverized coal in combustion. Coal micronized to a -325 mesh fineness would have almost three times more surface area than coal pulverized to a -200 mesh fineness. The benefits of the finer ground coal are: more rapid combustion; increased heat liberation; more uniform particle-to-air/oxygen contact; and increased heat flux distribution. Ideal's program, aimed at fuel conservation and improved refractory life, is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Roll crusher installation at Ciment Quebec Inc., St-Basile, Quebec
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The installation of a hydraulic roll crusher (HRC) at Ciment Quebec is described. The crusher size and capacity were selected to be high enough to feed five existing ball mills that have a combined installed power of 5750 hp. The HRC would allow more cement to be produced in a shorter period of time, utilizing a large winter stockpile of clinker, provide less dependence on cement storage capacity, and minimize the time impact of grinding high Blaine cement. The crusher installation was planned in several phases in order to minimize the project cost while meeting immediate production goals. The first phase included installation and operation of the crusher within five months of the initial contract. Succeeding phases are being executed at this time, and they include increasing the conveying capacity of the product transfer systems for all five mills. The maintenance and availability of the system have been very good. The integrity of the roll abrasion-resistant surfacing was initially a problem, but since August 1988, after a loss of several weeks of operation, it has not been a problem.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Modernization of cement mill no.11 at Southwestern Portland Cement Company, Victorville, California, plant
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The authors examine the operational aspects of the FLS/Koppern roller press installed at Southwestern Portland Cement Company's Victorville, California, plant. A review of the existing manufacturing facilities, a justification of the roll press system (its engineering and construction), and an evaluation of the initial operating experiences are included. It was found that, to obtain the full effect of the roll press, mill internals and ball charges should be redesigned. Recycling of separator reject back to the press in amounts up to 30% of total press feed, has not improved the system performance. Larger recycling of separator reject causes unstable operation of the press. Recycling of pressed flakes has a positive influence on the performance of the system. To date, up to a 35 to 40% increase in output has been achieved. It is projected that final modification and optimization will increase output by a total of 60 to 65% compared with performance before the high-efficiency separator and roll press.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Life extension for electrical power distribution systems using vacuum technology
publicationTitle: IEEE Record of Conference Papers on Cement Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is noted that, in industrial and utility electric systems built in the 1940s and 1950s, many components are at or beyond their expected service life. This is particularly serious in the case of power distribution equipment; failure comes without warning and often causes extensive damage to connected systems and other electrical equipment. Three alternatives for upgrading old equipment are discussed: total equipment replacement, utilization of used/remanufactured circuit breakers, and the retrofitting of existing circuit breakers. Retrofitting with vacuum arc interrupter technology is shown is shown to be the most cost effective and offers many advantages over older air-magnetic interrupters. These include simpler design, fewer parts and less maintenance, readily available parts, high reliability, extended insulation life, and safety. Modernization options available to industry, specifically in the area of electrical switchgear, are addressed. Emphasis is given to switchgear life extension using vacuum technology and its benefits, reliability, and economic justification. Several examples and applications are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
